ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The distance between two parallel metal rails is $L=0.40\mathrm{m}$, and the plane of the metal rails is inclined at an angle of $\theta=37^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Within the plane of the rails, there is a uniform magnetic field with a magnetic induction intensity of $B=0.50\mathrm{T}$, directed perpendicular to the plane of the rails. One end of the metal rails is connected to a DC power supply. A conductor rod ab with a mass of $m=0.040\mathrm{kg}$ is placed on the metal rails and remains stationary. The conductor rod is perpendicular to the metal rails and makes good contact with them. The current through the conductor rod is $I=1.5\mathrm{A}$, and $g$ is taken as $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$. It is known that $\sin37^{\circ}=0.60$ and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.80$.

1. What are the Ampere force and the frictional force acting on the conducting rod?
2. If the direction of the magnetic field is changed to be vertically upward, to keep the conductor rod stationary and free from friction, what is the magnitude of the magnetic induction $B_2$ at this time?
3. If the metal rails are smooth and the direction of the magnetic field can vary within the vertical plane, determine the minimum magnitude of the magnetic induction $B_3$ required to keep the conductor rod stationary.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two parallel metal rails placed in an inclined plane, and the rail plane makes an angle θ with the horizontal plane; the conducting rod ab spans the two rails and is perpendicular to the rails; the right end is connected to a DC power supply E and internal resistance r; in the figure, the arrow of the initial magnetic field B is perpendicular to the rail plane. From the shown current direction and magnetic-field direction, it can be judged that the initial Ampere force is along the rail plane in the uphill direction. Reasoning calculation: 1. The initial magnetic field is perpendicular to the rail plane, and the length of the conducting rod is equal to the spacing L between the two rails, so the magnitude of the Ampere force is F_A = BIL = 0.50 × 1.5 × 0.40 = 0.30 N. The component of gravity downward along the inclined plane is mg sinθ = 0.040 × 10 × 0.60 = 0.24 N. Because the Ampere force is uphill and greater than the component of gravity along the inclined plane, the static friction force should be downward along the inclined plane, with magnitude f = 0.30 − 0.24 = 0.06 N. 2. When the magnetic field is vertically upward, the Ampere force on the conducting rod is in the horizontal direction, and its component along the inclined plane is B_2 I L cosθ. Frictionless rest requires B_2 I L cosθ = mg sinθ, therefore B_2 = (0.040 × 10 × 0.60)/(1.5 × 0.40 × 0.80) = 0.50 T. 3. When the rails are smooth, only balance along the inclined-plane direction is needed. The magnetic-field direction may vary within the vertical plane; to make the required B smallest, the Ampere force direction should be exactly uphill along the inclined plane, at this time B_3 I L = mg sinθ, so B_3 = (0.040 × 10 × 0.60)/(1.5 × 0.40) = 0.40 T.
